title: Teaching on Purpose #21: Utilising Memory
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck opens the final purpose in the Chiltern Learning Trust framework, utilising memory, through a live conversation with English teacher Yamina Bibi. They begin with cognitive load theory, separating intrinsic, extraneous and germane load, and warn that working memory, long-term memory and load are constructs that should not be counted like objects. Kohlbeck adds that the aim is to optimise intrinsic load rather than maximise it. Bibi's chosen technique is a four-question retrieval grid covering last lesson, last week, last month and last year, deliberately linked to the theme of the coming lesson and extended back into the primary years to support the KS2 to KS3 transition. The piece argues that a predictable routine itself frees capacity, that scaffolds such as the academic sentence equation should be faded, and that Socratic dialogue can surface what pupils do not yet know. It closes by insisting that technique depends on the learners in front of us: the right thing, at the right time, for the right reason.
points: Cognitive load theory is most useful when treated as a set of constructs that guide decisions, not as a counting rule, and the goal is to optimise intrinsic load rather than simply maximise it.
Working memory capacity is not fixed, because expertise shrinks the space a topic occupies, which is why securely stored knowledge such as a well-practised recipe feels effortless.
A retrieval grid that spans last lesson, week, month and year works best when every question is tied to a theme of the coming lesson, so retrieval primes exactly the prior knowledge pupils will need.
Looking back beyond the current year, including primary content, builds a bridge for transition and shows why teachers benefit from visiting feeder schools.
Utilising memory is not only retrieval: fading scaffolds, Socratic dialogue that exposes gaps, and explicit teaching of genuinely new content all serve the same purpose depending on the learners.
quotes: We often hear that we should minimise extraneous load and maximise intrinsic load. But a working memory filled to the brim with intrinsic load is still an overwhelmed working memory. The aim is to optimise intrinsic load: the right amount of challenge at the right moment, not as much as we can squeeze in.
Capacity is not fixed for each person either. It depends on what you are thinking about. The same information takes up far less room for someone who already knows a lot about it.

Too often, both in her own teaching and in the lessons she has observed since, retrieval tasks and Do Nows have nothing to do with the content that follows. Yamina links every question in the grid to a theme that connects with what pupils are about to learn, so that retrieval brings to mind exactly the prior knowledge they will need.

But a routine like this does more than embed the gains of spaced retrieval. Its predictability means pupils come into the room knowing what is coming and feeling safe. That in itself frees up capacity for the thinking we actually want them to do.
It is worth remembering that working memory, long-term memory and cognitive load are all constructs. You could not scan someone’s brain and point to their working memory.

I think there is huge value in pupils feeling comfortable owning what they don’t understand. But, as always, it comes back to purpose. Sometimes I need to see the full range of misunderstandings in the room so that I can redirect the lesson.
Yamina does not see this as a choice between discovery learning and traditional teaching. She believes we need both.
